transcript:
Meeting: Developer Lift Off: Bootcamp - Auth, Env & SDK Demo
Date: 2025-08-12 15:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE); Maya Chen (Redwood SE); Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE); Evan Torres (ClearBridge Lead Eng); Priya Nair (ClearBridge Head of ML); Samir Gupta (ClearBridge CTO); Nora Blake (ClearBridge DevOps)

Summary:
Quick hands-on demo of Redwood SDKs (Python + TypeScript), auth options (API keys, service accounts, SSO/SAML), environment setup (CI secrets, sandbox), and a short tour of the Console + Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization. Agreed next steps to provision sandbox access and exchange security docs.

Topics:
- SDK install and quickstart (py/ts)
- Auth patterns: API keys vs service accounts vs SSO (SAML/OIDC)
- Environment/CI secrets and key rotation
- Console: model catalog, rollouts, traces
- Optimize: batching, kv cache, quantization recommendations

00:00 Jordan: alright everyone thanks for joining. this is jordan from redwood, i'm the account lead. we got about 45 minutes — wanted to run through a hands on bootcamp for your engineers, quick install, auth, couple samples in python and ts, and then how you'd run a small pilot. sound good?

00:22 Evan: yeah that's perfect. we're mainly focused on latency and also keeping token cost predictable, our product serves realtime answers to customers so 200-400ms p95 is our target.

00:37 Maya: great, we'll try to hit both. quick show of hands, who's going to be running infra vs app code?

00:45 Priya: samir and i will own model eval and prompt sets; nora will own infra/networking. evan will integrate the SDK into the api layer.

01:05 Jordan: awesome. show of quick starter — first step is pip/npm, env var for REDWOOD_API_KEY or you can use a service account token for dedicated/private. i'll drop the snippet repo after.

01:20 Maya: (sharing screen) okay i'll open the python quickstart. pip install redwood-sdk, then from redwood import Client, that's the pattern. simple code to stream tokens and handle stop sequences. we also show the async client pattern for high throughput.

01:40 Evan: is the streaming gRPC or websocket?

01:45 Liam: behind the scenes we have an HTTP/2 streaming endpoint and SDKs open a keepalive connection, it behaves like a websocket from app code. you can also do chunked responses from the REST endpoints if you prefer.

02:05 Priya: curious about kv cache — can i reuse cache across requests, we have long contexts.

02:12 Maya: yes that's our kv cache (sometimes transcribed as KV cash), you can persist and reuse keys between requests to save tokens. for private deployments it's the same API surface but you control TTLs.

02:35 Samir: networking — we will need VPC peering and SSO. how does redwood private handle SAML?

02:42 Jordan: for Private we support SAML SSO and OIDC; on Hosted you can connect via SSO + SCIM for user provisioning. for service-to-service we recommend rotating service accounts and KMS-backed keys.

03:05 Nora: we need details on KMS integration — can we use our cloud KMS / bring-your-own HSM?

03:12 Liam: yes, BYOK via customer KMS/HSM is supported in Private. for Dedicated we also offer KMS integration — note that audit logs and key usage metrics can be shipped to your logging account.

03:30 Evan: quick question about auth flows in CI: we use GitHub actions, how do you recommend injecting keys?

03:36 Maya: typical pattern — store service account token or short lived API key in your secrets store (GH secret or Vault) and mount into CI as env REDWOOD_API_KEY. we also suggest using short-lived tokens and automated rotation. we have sample GitHub Action workflow in the repo.

04:00 Jordan: okay i'm going to switch to the typescript example briefly. npm i @redwoodai/sdk or similar (note: transcript sometimes shows package name different). in TS you get typed responses and a dev server for local replay.

04:23 Evan: how do you handle token-level cost attribution — we need per-route metrics for billing internal teams.

04:30 Maya: Console provides token-level breakdowns, model-level usage, and route tagging. you can tag requests with route:customer-support or route:search. bills and console show cost per tag.

04:50 Priya: anything special for streaming vs batch pricing?

04:55 Liam: streaming uses token consumption similarly; batch throughput benefits from continuous batching and lower observed p99 by amortizing overhead. Optimize will give suggestions — we ran a quick estimate earlier for your typical 512-token completion and it suggested a 2.2x cost reduction if you enable prefix caching + dynamic batching.

05:20 Samir: can the optimize suggestions be automated? we don't want to babysit configs.

05:28 Maya: yes, Optimize can surface recommended batching windows and quantization profiles; you can accept suggestions or pin them to rollout policies. we also offer canary rollouts so you can test config changes on 5-10% of traffic.

05:45 Evan: ok let's do a short live install — can you walk through our pipeline?

06:00 Maya: sure i'll do python. starting repo: shared drive/redwood-starters/clearbridge-python. first create a virtualenv, pip install redwood-cli redwood-sdk. export REDWOOD_API_KEY=... or use redwood auth login to get temporary creds.

06:25 (screen) code: client = Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))

06:33 Evan: we like using service accounts so we can rotate keys regularly. do you have an endpoint for token introspection?

06:40 Liam: yes, for Dedicated/Private you can call the introspect endpoint to validate tokens and check scopes; we also support fine-grained scopes for embeddings vs generation.

07:05 Priya: data residency question — can we pin model serving to eu-west region?

07:12 Jordan: Hosted supports region selection per project; for Private you control region fully. we'll include region availability matrix in the security deck.

07:30 Nora: on the networking piece: VPC peering vs private link, firewall rules?

07:36 Liam: we support both VPC peering and cloud-provider private link equivalents. for peering we need your CIDR ranges and routing table details; we'll provide a template egress/ingress rule set.

08:05 Maya: back to code: showing a streaming example with async for chunk in client.stream_generate(...): process chunk. slight stutter — some names in transcript show toolkit as 'redwood sdk' or 'redwood client' inconsistently.

08:30 Evan: for long-running KV cache reuse, how do we authorize reading/writing caches?

08:36 Liam: you create a cache namespace and grant service account scopes to read/write; caches are encrypted at rest via KMS.

08:50 Priya: do you have example tests for quality/regression? we need to run prompt sets against model versions.

08:58 Maya: yes, there is an eval harness and you can upload prompt sets to Console; we run baseline comparisons and register regressions with alerts. you can attach a metric like exact-match or semantic-sim and get notified.

09:20 Samir: anything special about quantized models for latency? we saw notes about 4-bit quantization.

09:28 Liam: quantization helps with throughput and can reduce latency slightly depending on hardware. Optimize will suggest model variant + quantization tradeoffs given your latency/cost constraint. for extremely low latency we also provide pinned GPU pools in Dedicated.

10:00 Jordan: okay quick demo of Console — (screen) project view, model catalog, create environment, provision sandbox tokens. you can create a canary route and set rollout percent.

10:20 Evan: can we restrict model catalog visibility per team?

10:24 Maya: yes role-based access controls (RBAC) let you restrict models and routes per project or team. SSO + SCIM automates membership.

11:00 (15:12) Evan: small oddity — the SDK docs mention callback hooks for telemetry, is that available?

11:16 Liam: yes we have telemetry hooks that emit tracing spans to your APM; we also emit request ids in headers so you can correlate logs.

11:35 Priya: how are failures handled — fallbacks to smaller models?

11:40 Maya: built-in fallback policies allow you to route to cheaper/compatible model variants when a primary model is overloaded. there's also automated retry/backoff policies in the SDK.

12:00 Evan: demo looks good. can you show how to run an end-to-end CI job that runs prompts and verifies latency?

12:12 Maya: absolutely — sample GH action: setup python, pip install redwood-cli, run redwood evaluate --prompts=prompts.json --threshold=0.95, the action will fail if metrics degrade. we recommend running nightly smoke tests against a sandbox deployment.

12:45 Nora: for Private/on-prem, what's included in the air-gapped package?

12:52 Liam: air-gapped includes the runtime container images, orchestration manifests, and an installer. you manage the control plane and we provide upgrade packages. audit logs and billing metrics can be forwarded to your ELK or Splunk.

13:20 Evan: competitors — we evaluated openai and anthro — we liked redwood's cost controls and the unified runtime. any gotchas?

13:30 Jordan: main tradeoff is build vs buy — self-hosting gives control but more ops; Redwood aims to give predictable economics and lower ops for most teams.

13:50 Priya: one more nit: does the SDK support typed TS responses for structured outputs / function calling?

13:58 Maya: yes we have structured output helpers and function-calling primitives in both py and ts, with generated types for TS. sometimes the docs show slightly different naming but the patterns are stable.

14:20 Samir: good. let's recap next steps.

14:25 Jordan: recap — we'll provision a sandbox project, Maya will push starter repos, I'll send security and SOC2 docs, clearbridge will share prompt sets and latency targets. schedule a POC check-in for 2025-08-20.

14:45 Evan: sounds good. thanks everyone.

15:00 (end)

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcription missed a few product names (e.g., "Optimize" as "Opti-mize"), occasional speaker attribution errors, and some technical terms slightly garbled (KMS -> K-M-S, KV cache -> K V cash).
